title: Predicting problem gambling among online sports and race bettors: Assessing the value of machine learning using behavioural and self-reported data
authors: Heirene, R. M.; Vanichkina, D.; Zhang, E.; Huynh, E. L. Y.; De Leu, C. T.; Gainsbury, S. M.
tldr: Applies machine learning to predict high-risk gambling among 1,470 Australian online sports bettors, finding 30 days of behavioural data achieves AUROC 0.74-0.75 and survey data improves it to 0.85.
problem_and_motivation: Online gambling operators need effective risk detection systems, but optimal data windows and the value of combining behavioural with self-reported data remain unclear. Regulatory frameworks increasingly emphasize timely intervention, requiring clarity on minimal sufficient data.
approach: Collected survey data (PGSI, employment, income, gambling satisfaction) from 1,470 Australian sports and race betting customers.
Built machine learning models to classify participants into risk groups (PGSI 1-7 vs PGSI >=8).
Compared model performance using 30-day vs 6-month behavioural data windows.
Tested models with and without self-reported survey variables as features.
Identified most predictive account-based and self-reported variables.
findings: num: Behavioural-only models achieved AUROC 0.74-0.75 with similar performance across 30-day and 6-month windows.
num: Combining behavioural and self-reported data enhanced performance to AUROC 0.76-0.85.
Most predictive account-based variables: age, deposits per active day, average stake, days since betting.
Two self-reported variables drove improvements: number of gambling accounts and gambling satisfaction.
30-day behavioural data window is sufficient for adequate risk classification.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper demonstrates that machine learning models using only 30 days of behavioural data can adequately classify at-risk gamblers, with comparable performance to models using six months of data. It establishes that minimal self-reported variables (gambling accounts and satisfaction) can significantly enhance predictive accuracy. The work provides evidence that short data windows are sufficient for risk detection, supporting timely intervention requirements.
directly_justifies: 30 days of behavioural data achieves AUROC 0.74-0.75 for risk classification.
Adding two self-reported survey variables improves AUROC to 0.76-0.85.
Age, deposits per active day, and average stake are top predictive features.
limits: Sample limited to Australian online sports and race bettors (84.6% male).
Self-reported PGSI may not perfectly align with objective harm measures.
Results may not generalize to other gambling modalities or jurisdictions.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domain 5 (Profiles and Classification) was flagged as high relevance because ML classification of behavioral risk profiles is the core methodology. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged as high because the paper applies predictive ML to transactional data. All other domains (1-4, 7-14) were rejected.

limitations: Single-country, single-modality gambling context limits generalizability.
PGSI self-report as ground truth may misclassify some at-risk individuals. [unacknowledged]
No external validation of the model on holdout operators or time periods.
remember_this: 30 days of behavioural data suffices for adequate risk classification (AUROC 0.74).
Adding 2 self-reported variables improves AUROC to 0.85.
Deposits per active day and average stake are top predictive behavioural features.
Machine learning models can detect at-risk gamblers without protracted data windows.
